newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Tough tasks ahead for new Romanian govt-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Tough tasks ahead for new Romanian govt-analysts.

text.p: With reformists set to form their first government in Romania, analysts warned on Monday they will have to implement unpopular economic measures to rescue the Balkan country from its financial woes.
But they said a clear programme of change could take time to appear, with few politicians ready to dump populist promises before a run-off presidential election in two weeks time.
Romania's financial weakness, the prospect of a tough winter and the new government's ignorance of the real state of economy will also delay the start of change, they suggest.

"It will have to be a government of sacrifice whose successes will be judged according to the extent to which they manage to secure solid change even if social costs are high," independent economist Ilie Serbanescu told Reuters.
Romania's opposition Democratic Convention bloc (CDR) has a strong lead over its ex-communist foes in parliamentary polls.
First official results showed the CDR ahead in the parliament contest with some 30 percent, while President Ion Iliescu ruling leftist Party of Social Democracy scored 20.
To rule the CDR will need to negotiate an alliance with reform partners that will complicate economic decision making.
"The new government will have to rebalance the economy by restructuring, allowing prices to rise and accepting a further depreciation of the leu," Serbanescu said.

Restructuring and faster privatisation are targets Romania must meet under loan accords with the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. But so far Romania has done little to reshape the structure of its assets, a key factor for its credibility abroad and for foreign capital inflows.
"I could not find anything of what I think should be done in Romania immediately and necessarily in the platforms of any of the contenders," said Serbanescu.
Other analysts said electoral platforms will change when the reality of governing the country impinges but said it was too early to tell how events would unfold.
"It's premature to talk because we only have manifestos, not governing programmes," said one local economist.
Romania's voters appear to have liked the CDR's platform of tax cuts, increased pensions and loans for housing, improved land rights and better education.
But to put the economy on track the new government will have to give up such populist commitments. "At this stage, the economy simply cannot sustain such promises," Serbanescu said.
The CDR programme was short on detail and contained no costings. But analysts said the CDR would likely encourage foreign investment and take steps to modernise industry.
A healthy depreciation of the leu -- currently at an artificially high 3,410/25 to the dollar -- will be needed to bring it near prices in retail currency shops.
"Such measures will be hard as inflation was allowed to rebound (by the previous government)," Serbanescu said.
Inflation rose to a 12-month rate of 45.3 percent in September, compared with 27.8 percent last December and an expected end-1996 official target of 30 percent.
Romanians -- living on an average monthly wage of $100 -- are faced with a sharp drop in their purchasing power, which officially plunged by 30 percent from 1989, the year communists were ousted.
